messages.author: 34aa920e6230970b
messages.subject: Implementing Finite Mixture model of Royle and Nichols (2003, Ecology) in Stan
parts:
Hello.

Thank you for Stan. It is a great package.

I am trying to implement the Finite Mixture model of Royle and Nichols (2003 --- equation 5) in RStan. 

I have implemented the model in R, and can recover parameters from simulated data using optim:

#function to simulate data
sim_hpois <- function(n_sites, n_samples, p_oc, p_dt, seed = 42) {
  pop_sizes <- rpois( n = n_sites, lambda = -log( 1 - p_oc ) )
  n_detections <- sapply( pop_sizes, function(k) sum(rbinom( n = n_samples, size = k, prob = p_dt) > 0 ) )
  return( data.frame( N = pop_sizes, n_samples = n_samples, w = n_detections ) )
}

#function to calculate the log-likelihood
lhood <- function(parameters, data, max_k){
  r <- parameters[1]
  lambda <- parameters[2]
  K = seq(0, max_k)
  log_like <- function( r, lambda, K, R, w) {
    pk = (1 - (1 - r ) ^ K )
    prob = sum(dbinom( x = w, size = R, prob = pk ) * dpois( K, lambda = lambda ) )
    return( log( prob ) )
  }
  res = sum(apply( data, 1, function( x ) { log_like(r, lambda, K, x['n_samples'], x['w'])}))
  return(res)
}

# generate some toy simulated data
test_hpois <- sim_hpois( n_sites = 50, n_samples = 6, p_oc = 0.75, p_dt = 0.63 )

#estimate the ML
optim(c(0.1, 1), lhood, data = test_hpois, max_k = 100, control = list( fnscale = -1 ))
# this produces reasonable estimates that improve as we increase the number of samples.

# the crucial point is that we are summing over our uncertainty on populations size (defined by the K parameter), which could be anything from 0 to Inf,
# but for practical purposes usually good estimates can be obtained with values from 0 to 50 or 100

# here is my RStan --- perhaps naive ---- implementation!!

# my initial implementation was based on the manual's Finite Mixture suggestion, and using log_sum_exp function. But, that always failed to start. I suspect that the implementation of log_sum_exp was not 
# playing nicely with some -Inf values that inherently appear in the calculations when done on the log-scale, but should disappear once transformed to the normal scale. 
# so the below implementation is a close translation of the R code above.

learn_hpois <- function(data, lower_N = 0, upper_N = 20, iter = 2000, warmup = 1000, chains = 4) {
  K <- seq( lower_N, upper_N )
  data_list <- list(
                     n_points = length( K ),
                     n_ind = nrow( data ),
                     n_detections = data$w,
                     n_samples = data$n_samples,
                     K = K)
  hpois_model <- '
  data{
    int<lower=1> n_points; // 
    int<lower=1> n_ind; // number of surveyed birds
    int<lower=0> n_detections[n_ind]; // vector of number of detections
    int<lower=1> n_samples[n_ind]; // vector of number of tests
    int K[n_points];
  }
  parameters{
    real<lower=0> lambda; // distribution of abundance
    real<lower=0, upper=1> p_detect; // detection probability
  }
  model{
    real ps[n_points];
    real total;
    real theta;
    real diff;
    lambda ~ exponential(1); // prior on lambda
    p_detect ~ uniform(0, 1); // flat prior on detection prob
    diff = (1 - p_detect);
    for(i in 1:n_ind) {
      for(j in 1:n_points){
        theta = (1 - pow( diff, K[j] ));
        ps[j] = exp(poisson_lpmf(K[j] | lambda) + binomial_lpmf( n_detections[i] | n_samples[i], theta ));
      }
      total = sum( ps );
      target += log(total);
    }
  }
  generated quantities {
    real psi; // probability of occupancy
    psi = 1 - exp( -lambda );
  }
  '
  fit <- rstan::stan( model_code = hpois_model, 
                      data = data_list,
                      iter = iter, 
                      warmup = warmup,
                      chains = chains, init = list( list( p_detect = 0.5, lambda = 1 ) ) )
  return( fit )
}

# learn from the data
learn_hpois( test_hpois, lower_N = 0, upper_N = 50, iter = 2000, warmup = 1000, chains = 1 )


A copy-paste of the above code in R should be sufficient to reproduce what I have done.

The above code will run as long as lower_N > 0. Otherwise, the MH gets rejected too many times, and no chain is produced. Attempts to use print to help debug were fruitless, and no print statements are run until the chain gets going. So, I am wondering if I am missing some trick, or trivial change that could help this model run. Or, if the model is just not suitable for Stan.

Thank you for any help.

Best.

Anders.

Hi, I'm not sure but when K=0 your model is in a special case, where theta=0 so your binomial_lpmf will be - infinity if n_detections is not 0.  You might want to look at this K=0 case more carefully.

Hi, you want to avoid zero probabilities (or -infinity log-probabiliites) wherever possible.  You don't want a model assigning zero probability to something that occurs!
A

parts: I'd rewrite your loops:

for(i in 1:n_ind) {
tmp_d = n_detections[i];
tmp_n = n_samples[i];
ps = 0;
for(j in 1:n_points) {
theta = (1 - pow( diff, K[j] ));
if( theta > 0 && theta < 1 ) {
ps = ps + exp(poisson_lpmf(K[j] | lambda)
+ binomial_lpmf( tmp_d | tmp_n, theta ) );
} else if( theta == 0 && tmp_d == 0 ) {
ps = ps + exp(poisson_lpmf(K[j] | lambda) );
} else if( theta == 1 && tmp_d == tmp_n ) {
ps = ps + exp(poisson_lpmf(K[j] | lambda) );
} else {
ps = ps + 0;
}

target += log(ps);
}

as

vector[n_points] lps;
for (i in 1:n_ind) {
for (j in 1:n_points) {
lps[pos] = poisson_lpmf(K[j] | lambda)
+ binomial_lpmf(n_detections[i] | n_samples[i], 1 - pow(diff, K[j]));
target += log_sum_exp(lps);
}

This does a bunch of things. First and foremost, it
keeps everything on the log scale. It also accumulates
in a vector so that log_sum_exp is efficient. Finally,
it rejects rather than ignores the degenerate case of theta going
to 0 or 1 because the binomial will have a -infinity result.
As a bonus, it gets rid of all the temps (that's just style;
I think it makes it more readable to just use the variables and
keep the whole program shorter; I'd also get rid of the n_ prefixes
and rename n_ind to I and n_points to J, but that's just my preference
because I find short programs easier to read).

- Bob
